questions.q: Explain the main teachings of Buddhism.
answer: Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha in the sixth century BCE, at a time of great religious questioning, and its teachings offered a practical path to end human suffering.

answer.text: At the heart of Buddhism lie the Four Noble Truths. The world is full of suffering; suffering is caused by desire and craving; suffering can be ended by removing desire; and this can be achieved by following a set path. Thus the Buddha explained both the problem of suffering and its cure.

The path to end suffering is the Eightfold Path, which includes right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Because it avoids both indulgence and extreme austerity, it is called the Middle Way.
The Buddha stressed non-violence, right conduct and the attainment of nirvana, freedom from the cycle of birth and death, and rejected elaborate Vedic ritual and the authority of caste.

answer: These teachings gave Buddhism a wide and lasting appeal.

questions.q: Why did new religious ideas like Buddhism and Jainism emerge in the sixth century BCE?

answer.text: saw a great ferment of new religious and philosophical ideas, arising from changes in society and dissatisfaction with existing beliefs.

list: The rigid varna order and the dominance of Brahmanical ritual and animal sacrifice troubled many
The growth of towns, trade and a money economy created new classes seeking a simpler, more ethical faith
The Buddha and Mahavira, among others, taught ways to end suffering through right conduct rather than sacrifice
They rejected the authority of the Vedas and the caste basis of salvation, drawing wide support

questions.q: How did Buddhism spread, and what role did stupas and monasteries play?

answer.text: in and beyond India through teaching, royal support and its appeal to ordinary people.

list: The Buddha and his monks travelled and preached in the language of the people
Royal patrons, above all Ashoka, promoted it and sent missions to distant lands
Stupas built over the Buddha's relics became sacred places of pilgrimage and worship
Monasteries (viharas) housed monks and became centres of learning, helping the faith take root and spread
